o: Multiply two polynomials of degree up to 5·10⁴ with coefficients up to 10³ in absolute value; output coefficients can reach 5·10⁴·10⁶ = 5·10¹⁰, exceeding 32-bit but fitting in 64-bit. Naive convolution is O(nm) ≈ 2.5·10⁹ — too slow — so we use FFT-style methods. Because results must be exact integers, we either use NTT with two primes plus CRT (C++/Java) or Kronecker substitution packing coefficients into one big integer (Python/JavaScript BigInt).
k: Max output coefficient 5·10¹⁰ fits in 64-bit but not 32-bit — plan integer widths accordingly.
Two NTT-friendly primes (998244353, 754974721) have a product ≈ 7.5·10¹⁷ > 2·5·10¹⁰, so CRT reconstruction recovers the exact signed coefficient.
Kronecker substitution: pack coefficients into 64-bit blocks of one big integer; one native big-int multiplication performs the whole convolution since per-block sums stay below 2⁶³.

a.i: result[i+j] += poly1[i]·poly2[j] directly implements the definition. Simple and exact; use it to validate the fast method on small inputs, but it cannot pass the largest tests.

Number-theoretic transform convolves modulo each prime exactly; combining residues via CRT (with a final symmetric reduction for negatives) yields exact 64-bit coefficients. Alternatively, packing each coefficient into a 64-bit block of a big integer turns polynomial multiplication into a single big-int product, since block sums (≤ 5·10¹⁰) never overflow their 64-bit lane.
s: Pad both polynomials to the next power of two ≥ n+m−1.
(NTT route) Transform both, pointwise-multiply, inverse-transform, per prime; CRT-combine and fold values above half the prime product into negatives.
(Kronecker route) Pack coefficients into 64-bit little-endian blocks of a BigInt, multiply, unpack signed blocks.
a.t: O((n+m) log(n+m)) — three NTT passes per prime (or one big-int multiply, near-linear in practice)
a.sp: O(n+m) for padded arrays / big integers

w: Choose the method per language: Kronecker is by far the simplest exact approach where big integers exist (Python, JS BigInt); NTT+CRT is the portable high-performance route for C++/Java. Pitfalls: forgetting negative coefficients (normalize mod p, then symmetric CRT reduction), using a single NTT prime (998244353 < 5·10¹⁰ wraps results), and int overflow in accumulation. Sanity check with example 1: [3,2,5]·[1,4] = [3,14,13,20]. Follow-up: multiply many polynomials (product tree), or evaluate the result at a point without materializing it.
